    Burton admits he fathered a son out
    of wedlock
    Congressman's disclosure follows his pre-emptive strike

                                                          News

    By George Stuteville, John Strauss and Mary Beth Schneider
    Indianapolis Star/News

    This story is copyright ©1998, The Indianapolis Star and The

    INDIANAPOLIS (Sept. 4, 1998; updated 11 p.m. EST) --
    Rep. Dan Burton, alternately anguished and defiant, admitted
    Friday that he had an extramarital relationship with an Indiana
    woman and fathered a child by her in the early 1980s.

    Burton's confession came five days after he made an
    extraordinary and unexpected statement to his constituents at a
    town meeting that he had caused pain in his marriage. What's
    more, if the details came out, he would admit the truth.

            Oh, I see.  He would only admit the truth if more details come out.
 

    Friday, Burton made this admission:

    He had an affair.
 

          Staff photo / Ron Hoskins
          CENTER OF ATTENTION: Rep. Dan Burton talks
          with reporters on Friday evening in front of his
          Indianapolis home after announcing earlier in the
          day that he did have a affair in the early 1980's.
 

    He has a 15-year-old son he has never before publicly
    acknowledged as his.
 

        Wonder how a sensitive fifteen year old boy feels about something like this.  Seeing his father touting republican family values on television while treating him like dirt.  Lovely, danny burton, lovely. 

    He pays child support.

    He apologized for mistakes "that are mine and mine alone."

    But, Burton said, he was through talking.
 

        No you are not.  If Bill Clinton's not through talking, then you're not.

    "I'm not going to talk any more about my personal life. Enough is
    enough."
 

            "Enough is enough.."   Strange, coming from you.

    Hours later, though, Burton stood in the dark to talk to reporters
    in the driveway of his home.

    He spoke of the pain the sudden exposure has caused the
    families involved. "The boy was very, very upset," he said. "And
    I was concerned about the well-being of the mother, and the boy
    and their family, and what they were being put through."
 

        Well, he could have admitted it long ago so the child wasn't suddenly exposed to this.

    That, he said, is why he decided to tell the public of this
    long-hidden relationship.

    But he repeated: No more.

    Asked if this was his only sexual indiscretion, Burton said: "I just
    told you. I don't have any intention of going into every single
    rumor or allegation that may come up over the next week, two
    weeks or month."

    Burton will attend two town meetings in his district Saturday. But
    Jim Atterholt, Burton's district director, said that if constituents
    have questions about this matter, Burton will simply refer them to
    the statement he gave The Indianapolis Star on Friday.

    There would be no more explanations.

    Burton first made his admissions in the written statement and in a
    telephone interview with The Star.

    He said he wanted to go public to take the full criticism by
    himself and to deflect attention from the woman, their teen-age
    son and her family members.

    Out of deference to the boy and his mother, The Star and The
    News are not disclosing their names or their central Indiana
    hometown.

    The woman has declined to discuss her relationship with Burton,
    which occurred when he served in the Indiana Senate and the
    woman worked for a state agency.

    Provoked into admission
 

        Provoked into admission.  Gosh, I thought you republican family values people always always always told the truth fully and completely.

    Friday, in a telephone interview with The Star, Burton said the
    responsibility and blame is his alone, but he also criticized the
    White House and the media, charging they provoked the need to
    make his mistakes public.

    By heading a key House committee investigating President
    Clinton's campaign fund raising, he said he "joined a long list of
    individuals who have come under attack from people inside and
    outside of the Clinton administration."
 

        Oh, obviously a vast left wing conspiracy.

    The media, he said, "harassed innocent people in an effort to
    embarrass me" and asked "tasteless questions." Police, he said,
    had to force a television crew to leave the property of the
    woman.

    The White House had no comment on Burton's statement.
    However, spokesman Barry Toiv earlier dared Burton to
    produce evidence if he believed the White House was behind the
    media reports.

    "We have a lot of concerns about how Chairman Burton runs his
    investigation. His personal life is something we are not concerned
    with. We will aggressively address our differences with him and
    he will surely do the same with us," Toiv said.

    For the past two days, Burton has been in Indiana meeting with
    the woman and their son, and discussing the situation with his
    family and closest friends, many of whom have encouraged him
    to speak candidly.

        Wait a minute.  He had to be "encouraged" to speak candidly. 
He said he has also tried to prepare them for
    what he expects to be a traumatic aftermath.

    "I have tried to be as straight as I could be with my family on all
    this. I tried to keep it between my family and this lady's family,"
    Burton said.

    He called those discussions gut-wrenching and painful.

    "What bothers me the most is not about me. I know this is hard
    for someone to believe about a politician, but I have watched
    everybody's hearts being ripped out today," he said.
 

        Don't you think your other son's heart was ripped out every day, especially when he sees you and sees you display your "real" family.

    "I just don't want anybody to be hurt any more than they are
    going to be hurt. I made a mistake."

    He said his wife had been aware of the relationship.

    "I have accepted my full responsibility -- financial, everything. It's
    all been done in an agreeable way. There was no need for
    anybody to go to court or anything else. I said I would be glad to
    pay support because I think that is my responsibility."

    However, Burton has never officially acknowledged the boy as
    his son. His campaign literature only mentions the three children
    Burton has with his wife, Barbara. The boy's birth certificate
    does not list a father, and he has a different last name.
 

            Nice owning up there danny.

    While rumors about Burton's personal life had circulated for
    years, they reached a crescendo when a writer for Vanity Fair
    magazine began to interview hundreds of Burton's friends, family
    and political associates, along with current and former staff
    members.

    Some have said Burton opened himself up to having his personal
    life examined. Last spring, Burton -- a hard-line conservative
    who has been a longtime critic of the president -- called Clinton
    a "scumbag."

    He said that remark was never in reference to the president's
    now-admitted sexual relations with intern Monica Lewinsky. In
    fact, Burton maintains he has never made a public remark about
    Clinton's sexual misadventures.

    Friday, Burton sought to distance his situation and apology from
    the one President Clinton was forced to give in August.

    "I have never perjured myself. I have never committed
    obstruction of justice. I have been as straight as an arrow in my
    public duty. But this is private."

    The reaction

    Indiana Democratic Party Chairman Joe Andrew was only
    half-accepting of that.

    "I think this is a personal matter and a private matter," Andrew
    said. "But the underlying hypocrisy is what is troubling."
 

            Oh, that pesky old "H" word.

    Burton, he said, had made moralistic attacks on Democrats,
    accusing them of not standing up for the nuclear family when they
    said that families come in more than one shape and size.
 

        And little danny burton's family has a new interesting shape won't you say.

    "I would just hope that if any good can come of this, maybe Dan
    Burton would temper some of his moralistic outrage about other
    people's complex lives because he, too, has had a complicated
    life."

    Indiana GOP Chairman Mike McDaniel was out of state Friday
    and unavailable for comment.

    Bill Smith, a former aide to Burton and now executive director of
    the conservative Indiana Family Institute, said he was troubled
    by the congressman's admission that he had a child he had never
    owned up to before.

    "Of course it bothers me. I was unaware of it," Smith said.

    But he said he cared very much for Burton, a man he still
    respected, and trusted him as "a very caring, compassionate
    father and husband."
 

        How compassionate is it to ignore your own flesh and blood for political expediency.

    "I'd really like to talk to him myself," he said. In fact, Smith has
    about this matter -- twice before.

                        During Burton's 1982 campaign --
                        when Burton won after two
                        unsuccessful attempts -- Smith was
                        working on the campaign.

                        He heard rumors, he said, that his
                        candidate, then a state senator, was
                        "a skirt-chaser."

                        Campaigning door-to-door, Smith
                        recalled that "one woman told me she
                        could never vote for him because he
                        had done this and this and this.

                        "It bothered me. I went right to him. I
                        said I needed to know the truth."

    Burton told Smith there had been problems between himself and
    his wife and that he had gone out with other women -- or at least
    one other woman, said Smith, whose memory was hazy on the
    16-year-old conversation.

    "He said it in a way that alleviated my concerns," Smith said.

    Two or three years later, Smith was working as Burton's chief of
    staff and legislative director in Washington.

    "Some pastor said, 'How can you work for someone with his
    reputation?"' Smith said.

    "I went right back to Dan. He said, 'Bill, I've already told you
    about it. I'll probably live with that forever."'

    They never spoke of it again.

    "For about 7 1/2 years I was as close to Dan Burton as anybody
    could be," Smith said. "I never personally saw him in a
    compromising situation with another woman. Not once. He
    never did anything that in my mind was wrong."

    Rex Early, a former Indiana GOP chairman and a longtime friend
    of Burton, expressed sadness Friday night at the congressman's
    situation.

    "He's my friend. He's not just a political ally. He stuck his
    political neck out to endorse me knowing I was an underdog,"
    Early said, referring to his 1996 unsuccessful run for governor. "I
    don't forget things like that."

    Others may judge Burton, but Early won't. "It's unfortunate that
    something he did 16 years ago is an issue, but that's today's
    world of politics," Early said.

    Briane House, GOP chairman of the 6th Congressional District,
    which Burton represents, said he did not expect Burton's
    popularity there to be much dimmed.

            He will be elected by the same people who listen to rush and attack Bill Clinton for  his moral indiscretions. 
Instead of carrying the
    district by 93 percent in the November election, he might get
    only 90 percent of the vote, House predicted.

    Burton's core support comes, he said, from conservatives who
    are loyal and supportive.

    "Dan Burton could fill a gymnasium with them and they're not
    going to abandon him."

.
A CORNUCOPIA OF CORRUPTION
More Clinton Administration Scandals

By Edward Zehr

"Small crimes always precede great ones. Never have we seen
timid innocence pass suddenly to extreme licentiousness."

--Jean Baptiste Racine

There was a time, not so long ago, when the mention of Teapot
Dome at a Democratic National Convention could still provide a
mild degree of titillation to the assembled delegates. Wicked,
greedy Republican rubber barons -- we know all about them.
Watergate was the high-water mark for Democratic sanctimony. The
howling mob of party hacks and their boot-licking lapdogs in the
mainstream media must have known all about the ties that
Presidents Kennedy and Johnson maintained with organized crime,
but that did not prevent them hyping this "third-rate burglary,"
actually an ill-conceived, illegal phone tap, as the crime of the
century.

A cursory review of the latest crop of Clinton scandals reveals
how uneventful those "corrupt" Republican administrations really
were -- by comparison at least. The scandals involving Clinton
and his cronies revealed in a single month have outdone by a
wide margin all the scams perpetrated by the swindlers of Warren
G. Harding's administration. Is it time to rehabilitate the
reputation of President Harding? After all, nobody has ever
suggested the he took any part in the illegal activity that
occurred during his tenure or even had knowledge of it.

Nevertheless, Harding has been lumbered with full responsibility
for everything bad that happened while he was in office, unlike
Mr. Clinton who is routinely given a pass for each new scandal
that occurs under his grotesquely corrupt regime by the soporific
sentinels of the mainstream press. This, despite the fact that
Clinton has been accused under oath by several witnesses of
having involved himself in a major felony.

Harding, at least, was never sued for accosting a female employee
in his official suite. Clinton gets a pass on this as well, even
though he appears to have trouble keeping his trousers up in the
presence of the hired help. Needless to say, professional
"feminists" have been just as lax in waving their paladin through
the checkpoints as have the mainstream press. And why not? They
live by the same double standards and share the same hypocrisy.
What we have here is a generation of spoiled brats who were never
required to grow up. They take wallowing in emotional self-
indulgence as their due and recognize no responsibility to be
consistent or fair. Does anyone imagine for a minute that Richard
Nixon, or any other Republican president, could have survived a
scandal such as the Paula Jones affair (not to mention all the
others)?

The most recent Clinton administration scandals are too numerous
to be covered in a single column, but several of the affairs are
worth examining for the insight the provide into the progressive
degeneration of legality in government. In the latest round of
the campaign fund-raising investigation a dark cloud has
enveloped the vice president.


AL GORE'S TEMPLE OF DOOM?

The gist of this story is that Vice President Albert Gore Jr. was
present on four occasions at the Hsi Lai Buddhist temple in
Southern California when temple members gave illegal
contributions to the Democratic National Committee. New evidence
of this was recently revealed by investigators working on behalf
of the Senate committee, chaired by Sen. Fred Thompson (R-TN).
One of the events which DNC chairman Don Fowler assured the
committee was "not a fund-raiser," attended by Gore on April 29,
1996, "raised at least $166,000 for the DNC," according to Mary
Ann Akers of the Washington Times, who reported that,
"investigators plan to introduce evidence that the Hsi Lai temple
gave another $60,000 in illegal donations to the DNC at various
functions attended by both the president and the vice president."

Akers revealed that the investigators have hard evidence showing
that on Sept. 27, 1993, contributions totaling $5,000 were made
by three persons at another "donor-maintenance" event attended by
Gore at a law firm in Santa Monica, Calif. The problem with this,
according to Akers, is that, "It is against federal law to
reimburse contributors for donations made to political parties.
It is also illegal for tax-exempt, religious organizations to
make political donations."

In addition, Akers said that the investigators have determined
that the temple reimbursed contributors for:

"$25,000 to the DNC raised at a Feb. 19, 1996, event at the
Hay Adams Hotel in Washington attended by Mr. Clinton;"

"$5,000 to the party given at a 1995 event attended by both
Mr. Clinton and Mr. Gore;"

"$10,000 to the DNC given at a July 1996 event attended by
Mr. Clinton;"

"$6,000 given to the DNC at a Los Angeles event attended by
first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton."

One might wonder why a religious organization such as the Hsi Lai
Buddhist temple would be so deeply involved in Democratic
politics as to channel illegally laundered donations to the DNC.
It turns out that Maria Hsia, who organized the Santa Monica
event, is a "prominent political activist in the Asian-American
community," according to Akers, and a "confidante" of John Huang,
"the elusive former DNC fund raiser, [who] also funneled $45,000
into Democratic coffers from his former employer, the
Indonesian-based conglomerate Lippo Group..."

Both Hsia and Huang have invoked their Fifth Amendment rights to
avoid having to testify regarding the roles they have played in
the campaign finance scandal. Akers reported that aides to the
vice president "blamed the April 29 debacle on poor staff work
and bad communication."

To make matters worse, the DNC had only just acknowledged that
$120,000 in contributions solicited by Gore in a half-dozen phone
calls which he made from his office had been allocated by them to
the Democratic Party's "hard-money" account, not the "soft-money"
account as previously reported. Hard-money is used to finance the
campaigns of individual candidates -- the solicitation of such
funds on government property is illegal.

The danger in this for Gore is that Attorney General Janet Reno,
who has resisted appointing an independent counsel on the grounds
that Gore's solicitation of soft-money contributions is not
illegal, and thus does not require such an appointment, has now
had her rationale demolished and will probably be forced to
appoint one. (Murmurs about impeachment proceedings against Reno
have already been heard in the House). According to Reno, the
Justice Department first learned of the hard-money transfer by
reading the Washington Post. The Attorney General will be hard
pressed to continue avoiding the appointment of an independent
counsel in this case. A 1986 amendment to the independent counsel
statute requires that she would have to present "clear and
convincing evidence" that Gore "lacked the state of mind required
for the violation of criminal law involved."

The usually astute columnist Robert Novak said last week that
"Clinton political advisers" believe Reno has set a course that
"inevitably will trigger the independent counsel statute. At that
point, Gore will have lost control of his own political fate."

According to Novak, the White House had developed a strategy of
"preemptive dumping" of potentially embarrassing documents on the
news media before Thompson's Senate committee could disclose
them. This strategy has served Mr. Gore very badly.

Novak said that, "Gore defenders were horrified when Wednesday
morning's Washington Post was led by a story indicating the vice
president 'at a minimum' ignored warnings about the event at the
tax-exempt religious institution."

Investor's Business Daily reported that White House memos,
received by Gore at about the time of the fund-raising calls he
made from the White House last year "advised that some Democratic
Party donations would likely be deposited into 'hard money'
accounts." This contradicts Gore's claim that his calls did not
violate federal law.

The newspaper's account revealed that:

"The memos were sent by deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes to
President Clinton and Gore. Those memos, dated from Feb. 22
to July 28 of last year, explained that the first $20,000 of
donations from individuals were allocated to hard money
accounts."

Even in the face of this evidence, DNC lawyers continued to
maintain that Gore must have thought he was soliciting soft
money.


THE TAMRAZ PIPELINE

The Caspian Sea, located between Southeast Europe and Asia, just
north of Iran, has enormous oil reserves, estimated at 200
billion barrels. Roger Tamraz, described as "an American citizen
with a shady and untrustworthy reputation" in a memo sent to the
DNC by Vice President Gore's office, "holds two Caspian oil
concessions believed to contain 1 billion barrels," according to
the Washington Post. The Post mentioned in a Sept. 9 article by
David Ottaway and Dan Morgan that Tamraz is "a fugitive from
Lebanon, where he is wanted on 1989 charges of embezzling $200
million."

Tamraz attributes these allegations to political rivals in
Lebanon. An attempt by the Lebanese government to have Tamraz
extradited through Interpol seems to have been ignored by most
Western governments. U.S. officials have told the Post that the
Clinton administration has not taken action because this country
has no extradition treaty with Lebanon.

Since the early 1990s, Tamraz has been promoting a pipeline to
carry oil from the Caspian to a port in Southeastern Turkey. This
would greatly enhance the value of his property. The route he
proposed would also avoid Russia and Iran, consistent with U.S.
policy. The Post reported that:

"On Sept. 11 and Sept. 15, [1995] Tamraz attended political
functions with Clinton, and on Sept. 18, the DNC recorded a
$50,000 contribution, bringing his total to at least $95,000
to the party."

On Oct. 6, Tamraz met with DNC chairman Fowler. He had met with
two Democratic fund-raisers at the Four Seasons Hotel in
Georgetown on the same day. After contributing $95,000 to the
Democratic Party, Tamraz felt that he was entitled to have access
to the vice president and other senior administration officials,
but he had just been prevented by Gore's aides from attending a
political breakfast. The two fund-raisers, DNC finance director
Richard Sullivan and finance chairman Marvin Rosen, told Tamraz
that they would require a little more time to overcome resistance
to receiving him in the White House, according to the Post.

Within two weeks of the meeting, Tamraz made an additional
contribution of $75,000 to the Virginia Democratic Party. The
Post said that the donation was made "at the request, according
to two sources, of DNC chairman Donald Fowler."

The Post report continued:

"Far from being ostracized, Tamraz was then admitted to four
White House functions, including a dinner with President
Clinton at which Tamraz touted his pipeline and the jobs it
would bring to U.S. pipe manufacturers."

Columnist William Safire wrote that, "After one direct pitch,
Clinton told his sandbox crony Mack McLarty to put in a good
word for Tamraz at the Energy Department, a corrupt order that
McLarty carried out."

Phil Kuntz, writing in the Wall Street Journal, said that Tamraz
was a long-time CIA asset. Kuntz wrote:

"According to Mr. Tamraz's testimony, he met regularly with
CIA operatives for 25 years, until becoming ensnared in
controversy. A naturalized American citizen from Lebanon, he
says he provided information about the Middle East and
elsewhere to as many as 25 CIA officials over the years."

Safire reported that "At Tamraz's direction, fund-raiser Fowler
twice spoke to the C.I.A. agent known as 'Bob.'"

Fowler told Thompson's Senate committee that he cannot remember
any such contact. Safire noted wryly, "Perhaps Bob and colleagues
sprinkled intelligence holy water over this fugitive oilman,
because warnings that Tamraz had 'significant financial and
ethical problems' were overridden."

The methods employed by Mr. Tamraz would seem to be effective,
but are they ethical? If the CIA had information that influence-
peddling was going on were they not obliged to pass this
information along to a higher authority? Safire asked this
question of William Lofgren, Bob's boss at the "C.I.A.'s
Directorate of Operations, fondly remembered as the Department of
Dirty Tricks."

"We sent a memo that told of Fowler's call to poor Bob up to the
Seventh Floor," Lofgren replied. "The routing sheet was to
everybody, but now they say nobody ever saw it."

Safire dryly noted that Lofgren, "after 30 years of clandestine
service," quit the agency in 1996 "and became a consultant for
three months to -- you guessed it -- Roger Tamraz."

Next Safire asked John Deutch, who was Director of Central
Intelligence at the time, whether he had been informed. Deutch
told him that he is certain he had not been informed, "and seemed
fairly certain that George Tenet, then his deputy and now his
successor as D.C.I., also was not informed of this rogue
operation."

Deutch also told him that "Any unauthorized contact between
anyone in the Directorate of Operations and the D.N.C. was a
serious abuse of the political system."

Safire commented "if Samuel Berger, then Deputy N.S.C. Director,
was too docile at Clinton-Gore campaign meetings to object to
arms dealers, drug dealers and oil promoters being sold the run
of the White House -- then something terrible is happening."

William Lofgren stated it more succinctly: "Our threshold of
outrage has been raised."

Indeed, something terrible is happening. Our threshold of outrage
has been raised above anything that would have been imaginable a
few short years ago. For an illustration of how low our
government has actually sunk, read on.


DIRTY TRICKS AT THE APEC CONFERENCE

If the preceding example illustrates a serious abuse of the
political system, the one that follows demonstrates the extent to
which this government has criminally misused its intelligence
gathering capability. As usual, the mainstream press have bailed
out on this one, leaving the story to be reported by a few
borderline and alternative media outlets. They seem to do this
every time the story gets really ugly, or involves revelations
that cannot be rationalized with the usual mealy-mouthed double-
talk, situational "ethics" and similar specious twaddle.

The September 16 Washington Times carried a story by Greg Pierce
that very briefly outlined an intelligence operation carried out
by the "FBI and other U.S. intelligence agencies" at the Asia-
Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting that took place in Seattle
in 1993. President Clinton made an appearance at the conference.

The operation involved bugging the rooms of foreign officials who
were attending the meeting. Restaurants, rental cars and the
chartered boat that took Mr. Clinton and other national leaders
to a salmon feast on Blake Island were also bugged. It has been
alleged that this information was passed, by way of the White
House, to "the DNC, officials and outside attorneys working for
the Democratic Party -- information of great importance to high-
stakes private business deals with Asian countries," according to
an article that appeared in the September 29 Insight magazine.
This suggests the possibility that such information might have
been traded for foreign campaign contributions.

The Washington Times said that the magazine cited "sources who
claim direct knowledge of the operation." Official sources
either declined to comment or denied having any knowledge of such
an operation. That is what might be called the sanitized version
of the story. The article that appeared in Insight magazine,
written by Tim Maier, included allegations that were not
discussed in the Times article. For example, Maier mentions "an
apparent failure by federal law-enforcement and intelligence
authorities to pursue allegations of kickbacks to FBI agents
involved in the sweeping intelligence operation."

In a September 9 appearance on Jim Quinn's radio program, Maier
said that three commercial companies supplied the large number of
listening devices used in the operation and that part of the
price was kicked-back to the purchasers. In his article Maier
wrote that "those said to have engaged in kickbacks involving
thousands of dollars include FBI agents through suppliers with
whom they worked to procure electronic audio- and video-
surveillance equipment."

Maier said that "high officials in and out of government who
claim direct and indirect knowledge of the APEC bugging" cited
this as one reason for the cover-up. He said that the FBI agents
involved justified the kick-backs as compensation for hundreds of
hours of unpaid overtime. Maier noted that a Seattle grand jury
had investigated similar allegations connected with prior cases,
but did not indict any of the FBI agents involved.

According to Maier, intelligence authorities also failed to
pursue allegations "involving underage boys provided as
prostitutes to visiting dignitaries attending the week-long
November conference of 15 Asia-Pacific nations."

Maier told Quinn, "Video cameras confirm that young, under age,
boys were supplied for the 'enjoyment' of aides and staffers
attending the APEC conference. Several rooms were set aside in
one hotel." He said that the boys were American and that the
procurer had not been identified, nor had the judge who
authorized the surveillance. He also told Quinn that it was the
use of the boy prostitutes and the passing of intercepted
conversations to the DNC that induced some agents to blow the
whistle on the operation.

Regarding the coverup of child prostitution by the government,
Maier wrote:

"Despite the protestations by FBI agents who uncovered this
exploitation, supervisors in the Seattle field office of the
FBI--as well as supervisors and managers at FBI headquarters
in Washington--refused to mount a criminal investigation or
support local prosecution. Instead, according to one source,
the FBI agents 'were told to forget about it' because
arresting the men involved with the children 'would
jeopardize the national-security mission.'"

Joseph Farah observed in World Net Daily, "nobody's commenting at
the White House or at the FBI or at the National Security Council
or at the Secret Service or at the DNC. Mum's the word." Farah
took this as an indication that stonewalling, which failed to
work for Nixon, works a treat for the Clinton administration.


Could this be due in part to the extraordinary lack of curiosity
most mainstream journalists seem to have regarding the Clinton
scandals? And could that perhaps be conditioned by the perception
that too much curiosity about such things is not career
enhancing? Examples such as that of Mr. Kelly, until recently
editor of the New Republic, have no doubt had a chilling effect
upon those reporters whose natural inclination might lead them to
delve too deeply into such matters. And the admonition of Mr.
Kaplan to his CNN news staff not to use the word "scandal" so
often in referring to stories involving this administration are
unlikely to rekindle their zeal for investigative reporting.

Maier wrote that his sources "were appalled and amused" at the
reactions of official government spokesmen regarding their
revelations. According to Maier:

"Those claiming direct knowledge say this is why they came to
Insight, and that only action by the appropriate
congressional committees and a federal grand jury can get to
the bottom of allegations involving official crimes and a
national-security operation gone awry."

Don't hold your breath. As Farah observed, citing Mr. Gore, there
would appear to be "no controlling legal authority" in this
matter.

Those who have convinced themselves that character doesn't matter
and that there is no harm in turning a blind eye to the "minor"
infractions of law committed by their brave lads, should realize
that political corruption feeds upon itself. Public officials who
are allowed to get away with flouting the law on a small scale
are emboldened to move on to greater outrages. This did not begin
in 1993 -- it has been going on for a long time, and the
consequences are becoming all too clear. If we do not begin to
demonstrate zero tolerance for government corruption -- and soon
-- our entire political system will be at risk.

WHITE HOUSE 'BACK DOOR' OPENED
WITH CASH TO DEMOCRATS

Scripps Howard News Service
Release date: 09-12-97

By LANCE GAY
Scripps Howard Staff Writer

WASHINGTON -- President Clinton's national
security adviser said Thursday that the White
House was unprepared for how foreign
businessmen would use the Democratic National
Committee as a back door for getting into the
White House.

``We did not see this problem on the radar
screen,'' National Security Council director
Sandy Berger told the Senate Governmental
Affairs Committee investigating campaign
finance abuses.

Berger said it was not customary, until he
adopted new policies this year, to check on the
backgrounds of foreigners entering the White
House. ``It was not the practice of the NSC or
the White House for 30 years,'' he said.

Sen. Fred Thompson, R-Tenn., chairman of the
panel, said Chinese arms dealers, shady
Russians connected with organized crime, and
businessmen with connections to Chinese
Communist government officials were able to get
into DNC-sponsored coffees and dinners with
Clinton through contributions made to the
Democratic Party.

Berger agreed the NSC failed to protect the
president ``as a living stop sign'' to keep
foreigners from getting unwarranted access.
``Some things happened in 1995-96 that, in
hindsight, should not have happened,''
he said.

Berger himself was drawn into the process after
former DNC Chairman Don Fowler arranged for
Hong Kong businessman Eric Hotung to have
his picture taken with Berger in the White
House in October, 1995. A week after the
picture was taken, Hotung's wife, Patricia,
contributed almost $100,000 to the DNC.
Patricia Hotung is an American citizen, but
Hotung is a citizen of Hong Kong.

Berger said he met with Hotung only on the
advice of Robert Suettinger, a CIA analyst who
formerly worked at the NSC as the senior Asia
coordinator, and who had met Hotung.

An NSC staff memo prepared for Berger about
Hotung read, ``The guy is straight out of (the
novel) 'Taipan' in terms of his life story, but a bit
off the wall.''

Berger said he did not know of the Hotung
contribution, and had he known, would not have
agreed to the photo. He also was approached
later by Fowler to write a letter to Democratic
contributor George Chu detailing the Clinton
administration's policy on China and the United
Nations, but did not respond to that request.

Senate investigators are laying out evidence
showing that businessmen blocked from
meeting Clinton when they approached the
White House found a convenient back door
through the DNC.

Thompson questioned the value of the photo to
Hotung, since Berger is not a major political
figure even in Washington. ``The photograph
was worthless,'' Berger agreed.

Sen. Don Nickles, R-Okla., noted that
Lebanese-American businessman Roger Tamraz
was able to meet six times with Clinton in 1995
and 1996 even after the NSC had ruled that it
would be improper for Tamraz to meet any
senior U.S. government officials. Tamraz was
seeking Clinton support for an oil pipeline from
the Caspian Sea to Turkey, a project NSC
officials warned could disrupt relations with
Russia.

According to documents released by the
committee, after one of the DNC dinners,
Clinton directed Tamraz meet with Clinton's aide
Mack McLarty. McLarty told Clinton in an April 2,
1996 memo, ``Roger was very pleased with your
interest, and we will follow-up in a supportive,
but very prudent and appropriate way.''

Berger said the whole system for getting people
in to see the president should be improved.

``I felt very strongly that we needed to have a
much clearer system, much more clarity for our
staff people, so that there would not be any
questions about how these things should be
handled,'' he said.

Berger who served as Clinton's campaign
manager in 1992, said he attended weekly
campaign strategy meetings with Clinton's
political staff during the 1996 campaign. Berger,
who then was No. 2 on the NSC staff, said he
wanted to ensure that campaign advertisements
and speeches didn't distort Clinton's foreign
policy stands.

Sen. Carl Levin, D-Mich., noted President
Bush's national security adviser, Brent
Scowcroft, attended twice daily political meetings
at the White House when Bush was running for
re-election in 1992. Berger's involvement in the
political campaign, he said, was not unusual.

(Lance Gay is a reporter for Scripps Howard
News Service.).

dismissed on national security grounds and two
officials who received unprecedented pre-trial
pardons by President Bush following his electoral
defeat in 1992. Two of the convictions were
reversed on appeal on constitutional grounds
that in no way cast doubt on the factual guilt of
the men convicted. The individuals charged and the
disposition of their cases are:

(1) Robert C. McFarlane, National security advisor
1983 to 1985: pleaded guilty to four counts of
withholding information from Congress;

(2) Caspar W. Weinberger, Secretary of Defense:
charged with four counts of false statements and
perjury; pardoned before trial by President Bush.

(3) Elliott Abrams, Assistant secretary of state
for inter-American affairs 1985-1989: pleaded
guilty to withholding information from Congress;

(4) Oliver L. North, Deputy director for
political-military affairs at the National
Security Council: convicted of altering and
destroying documents, accepting an illegal
gratuity, and aiding and abetting in the
obstruction of Congress; conviction
reversed on appeal;

(5) John M. Poindexter, Deputy national security
advisor under McFarlane 1983 to 1985: convicted of
conspiracy, false statements, destruction and
removal of records, and obstruction of Congress;
conviction reversed on appeal;

(6) Richard V. Secord, Retired Air Force general
responsible for early transfer of weapons to Iran:
pleaded guilty to making false statements to
Congress;

(7) Albert Hakim, Secord's partner beginning 1983:
pleaded guilty to supplementing the salary of
North;

(8) Thomas G. Clines, a retired CIA agent:
convicted of four counts of tax-related offenses
for failing to report income from the operations;

(9) Carl R. Channell, prominent fund raiser and
lobbiest for Contra causes: pleaded guilty to
conspiracy to defraud the United States;

(10) Richard R. Miller, Major player in political
and paramilitary operations with North and
Channell: pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud
the United States;

(11) Clair E. George, During 1980s deputy director
of CIA responsible for covert operations:
convicted of false statements and perjury before
Congress;

(12) Duane R. Clarridge, Top CIA official in
charge of covert Nicaraguan war, 1981-1984:
indicted on seven counts of perjury and false
statements; pardoned before trial by President
Bush;

(13) Alan D. Fiers, Jr, Succeeded Clarridge in
1984 as CIA official in charge of day-today covert
operations in Central America: pleaded guilty to
withholding information from Congress;

(14) Joseph F. Fernandez, CIA: indicted on four
counts of obstruction and false statements; case
dismissed when Attorney General Richard L.
Thornburgh refused to declassify information
needed for his defense;


At the time President Bush pardoned Weinberger and
Clarridge, he also pardoned George, Fiers, Abrams,
and McFarlane.

Democrats begin to discuss Clinton resignation

9/5/98

Ron Fournier, Associated Press Writer

WASHINGTON (AP) -- Gingerly reflecting their
disappointment and anxiety, some Democratic leaders
across the country are beginning to discuss the
possibility that President Clinton should resign if the
Starr report to Congress threatens the party agenda and
its fall campaigns.

Though still sticking by the president, their sentiment
was summed up by New Hampshire party chairman Jeff
Woodburn: ``You can't be blindly loyal.''

With voices rising in Democratic ranks, some White
House advisers say a congressional censure may be a
best-case-scenerio for Clinton after prosecutor Kenneth
Starr releases his report on the Monica Lewinsky affair
and alleged cover up.

Iola McGowan, vice chairwoman of the Illinois
Democratic Party, said the president should at least be
censured. ``We do need something to put this behind us,''
she said.

One longtime Clinton adviser, speaking on condition of
anonymity Friday, said an abruptly shifting political
landscape may prompt him to urge the president ``to take
the honorable way out'' and resign.

No Democrat said for attribution that Clinton should
resign, only that it was now a possibility. Most party
officials still argue that Clinton has had little impact on
congressional races -- and need not consider stepping
down.

``There are always people who want to cut and run, but
Bill Clinton should be permitted to move forward,'' said
Ed Marcus, chairman of the Connecticut Democratic
Party. ``Now is not the time to be piling on,'' said Gary
LaPaille, an influential Democratic National Committee
member from Illinois.

At the White House, where aides say Clinton is giving
no thought to resignation, spokesman Barry Toiv said
most of the evidence suggests that Clinton's problems are
not hurting Democratic candidates.

``It's understandable that the atmosphere that's been
created in recent days could cause some anxiety, but if
candidates focus on what Democrats have accomplished
and what they want to achieve in the next two years, that
will be their best formula for success,'' Toiv said.

But interviews with Democratic leaders across the
country showed clearly growing anxiety that Starr's
report may reveal new details that weaken the president's
grip on office or create a congressional frenzy that
freezes out the Democrats' message to voters.

Whispers of resignation surfaced last week as party
operatives fretted over ominous signs in polls that could
portend a strong turnout for Republicans in Nov. 3
elections -- and significant losses for Clinton's party.
Several key Senate Democrats voiced their concerns
about Clinton in remarks from the Senate floor and
House members return from August recess this week
carrying concerns from their constituents and eager to
see a new set of pre-election surveys.

The tide began to turn against Clinton when Democratic
Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a longtime Clinton ally, declared
on the Senate floor Thursday that the president's actions
demanded a formal ``public rebuke.''

While the Connecticut lawmaker spoke of the president's
morality and its impact on ``our national character,'' some
Democrats said they feared the political implications of
Clinton's actions.

``There is such disappointment ... because we all believe
if Democrats do well (in November), we will have better
public policy,'' said Woodburn. ``I didn't do this to
defend sexual exploits of the president. And at some
point in time we all have to ask ourselves are we helping
the cause that motivates us to do this or are we simply
holding on to power?''

``The cause is important,'' he said. ``You can't be blindly
loyal. You have to be loyal to the cause.''

Woodburn said he felt sorry for ``the little old ladies
who defended (Clinton) in bridge clubs.'' Yet he said
most people don't want Clinton to leave office.

Philip Perington, the Colorado party chairman, said,
``We've just taken a wait-and-see attitude. We really
haven't taken a position other than it's Clinton's problem
and if it becomes a problem for our candidates and our
leadership than he really needs to assess where the party
will be in the next two years and take a long view of
what's down the road, and look at it from the party's
view.''

``He's got the ball,'' Perington said.

Some Democrats are worried about what shoe might drop
next.

Clinton ``knows what's going to come out in the report.
We don't,'' said Pauline Woods, a DNC member and
former vice chairwoman the Georgia Democratic Party.
``If it's something that will hurt every candidate, he needs
to step down. If not, he needs to stay and fight.''

McGowan, the Illinois Democrat who talked of censure,
said, ``I think we should wait and see the whole (report)
and then we can see whether he should resign -- or
whatever he should do.''

John Norris, Iowa's Democratic chairman, said it comes
down to whether Clinton can advance his policies. ``If he
can't move forward, he's got to make that decision,''
Norris said, adding that he's seen no impact yet on Iowa's
campaigns. ``If he feels that way, he's got to make the
decision to step down. That's not for me to do.''

The senior Clinton adviser urging resignation said many
Democrats fear the revelation of ``weighty circumstantial
evidence'' in the Starr report. ``Now is the time to take
the high road, before the report,'' the adviser said. ``He'd
be well advised to leave and say, `I can't do the job
people hired me to do.'''

The adviser has talked to the president since his Aug. 17
acknowledgment of an affair with Ms. Lewinsky but has
not broached the subject of resignation.

Democratic pollster Mark Mellman said party officials
talk openly of resignation because Republicans are
predicting a 20-seats gain in the House thanks to
Lewinsky fallout. Like many Democrats, he says the
figure is inflated.

``I think there's a certain amount of unjustified panic
setting in,'' Mellman said.

David Leland, chairman of the Ohio Democratic Party,
said resignation talk ``is way, way, way too premature.
The president has done a good job of being president and
we should support him in that role.''

His counterpart in New Hampshire, Woodburn, was
asked if the party would be better off with Vice
President Al Gore as president the next two years. He
paused for the count of five, took a deep breath and said
Clinton's resignation would probably not prevent the
Lewinsky affair from dominating the elections anyhow.

Will Clinton survive?

``Today, yes,'' the chairman said. ``Today. But
tomorrow's tomorrow. The next day's the next day. A
whole lot can change.''

Wednesday, September 23, 1998

PERSPECTIVE ON THE WHITE HOUSE SCANDAL
Public Anger Rises Over Starr's Abuses
America outside the Beltway has to make Congress see at last
that this
attack on democracy must end.
By CAROL TAVRIS

Los Angeles is the city that gave the nation its
first example of
scandalous behavior on videotape (the LAPD beating
of
Rodney King), its first example of sexual hysteria
in a
day-care scandal (the McMartin case), its first target in
an official
government witch hunt (the Hollywood 10, which launched
McCarthyism) and the one case where conclusive DNA
evidence
was rendered inconclusive (the O.J. Simpson trial). We're
the city of
dreams and delusions, manufacturer of artifice and image.

Bill Clinton should be our poster boy--sex, lies,
videotape, sexual
hysteria, DNA and a witch hunt rolled into one juicy
story. Yet,
curiously, newspapers here are doing better at telling
the real story
beneath the media-hyped one, quite different from what
folks on the
East Coast are getting. For example, on the day that one
Eastern
newspaper's headline was "Painful Debate Over Clinton's
Future
Begins: Nation Showing Its Dismay and Reluctance; Censure
Gets
Closer Look," the Los Angeles Times' headline was
"Public's Support
of President Found to Remain Strong: . . . Numbers show
Starr took
bigger personal hit than did Clinton."
Over and over again, the majority of the public,
nationwide, has
made it clear that they think impeaching a man for having
a sexual
affair and lying about it is inappropriate and
ridiculous. Of course,
many despair about Clinton's astonishing hubris in
assuming he
wouldn't be caught, and many joke about his stupidity in
pursuing an
affair with an infatuated, conniving tchotchke like
Monica Lewinsky.
But most have said repeatedly that they are angrier at
Kenneth Starr,
whose reckless obsession to bring down Clinton makes
Ahab's
pursuit of the whale look like a fishing expedition.
Yet none of these consistent surveys seems to
matter. The
Republicans escalate their moral crusade, their prattle
about
bipartisanship and their own sexual hypocrisies to the
contrary
notwithstanding. The media, their teeth on a story that's
worth O.J.
Simpson, Princess Diana and Chappaquiddick rolled into
one, aren't
about to let go.
The result, from where I sit, is a groundswell of
public anger and
fear for the future of the republic such as I haven't
seen since the
divisive days of Vietnam. Congress can censure or impeach
a
president for an abuse of power; where, the public
wonders, are the
controls on Starr's abuse of power? Why is Congress not
concerned
about the "high crimes and misdemeanors" committed by the
special
prosecutor's office: the coercion of testimony, the
invasion of privacy
of private citizens as well as the president, the
hounding of innocent
people in Arkansas to try to dig up dirt on Clinton, the
leaks to the
press?
But there is a big difference between how people
felt during the
Vietnam era and how many feel now: Then, both supporters
and
opponents of the war felt they had a voice and that their
voice
mattered. Opponents had a specific goal: Stop the war.
Today, many
people feel helpless to slow, let alone stop, a
governmental
juggernaut: How can we possibly organize an "enough,
already!"
campaign?
In social psychological terms, the nation is caught
in an emotional
contagion--excitement, news, endless talk and analysis,
all feeding on
one another and generating more of the same--and such
contagions
have no logical stopping point.
What will help us achieve closure on Bill Clinton?
First, Congress
can vote on whether to officially censure Clinton for his

"inappropriate" and "immoral" sexual behavior and for
lying to save
his skin. This will allow everyone to feel they have
taken the moral
high road. Second, Congress should officially thank Starr
for all that
time and money spent to bring a sexual rascal to justice.
Then
Congress should pass a resolution instructing Janet Reno
to fire him.
This will allow everyone to feel that the $45 million was
well spent,
while congratulating themselves on saving the taxpayers
the next $45
million Starr would run up.
If Congress fails to take these steps toward
closure, defying the
wishes of the American majority, then it will be left to
the public to
send a resounding message to the pollsters and to
Republicans this
election: We have had enough of this moral crusade, this
fascistic
effort to bring down a legally elected government. If the
public
remains angry yet apathetic, I fear not only for the
president, but for
the presidency; not only for the Democrats, but for
democracy.
- - -

Carol Tavris Is a Social Psychologist Who Writes
Frequently on
Behavioral Research

Thursday, September 24, 1998

Starr's Tactics Win Sympathy for Clinton
White House scandal: A fake populist is getting the
benefits of a populist
revolt.
By ALEXANDER COCKBURN
Latino storekeeper on New York's lower East Side shook
his head in disgust as he watched the president testify to the
grand jury. His anger was not at Bill Clinton but at Ken Starr
and his team of prosecutors. "It's just like when they get those kids
down to the police station, and they ask them the same thing over and
over, anything to try and trap them." One poll taken after the
broadcast of the president's testimony showed that the approval for
Clinton's job performance actually jumped from 59% to 68%, a
register of the disgust felt by ordinary Americans--in sharp contrast
to the opinion-forming elites--at what Clinton has been forced to go
through.
Ordinary people don't like the intrusions into Clinton's personal
life. They think his misbehavior in this area is irrelevant to the
performance of his job. And increasingly, I suspect, Americans are
registering a larger disgust at prosecutorial techniques.
There's a useful parallel to be made here with the last great
judicial spectacle, the O.J. Simpson trial. Many whites raged at
widespread black support for Simpson and tried to establish a false
solidarity with the poor by denouncing "rich man's justice." It didn't
wash with blacks, the vast majority of whom had family members,
friends or acquaintances mashed in the wheels of the justice system,
and who rooted for O.J. because, with his resources, he at least
might beat the system that had blighted so many lives.
Ditto with Clinton, with whom blacks in particular overwhelmingly
sympathize in his present troubles. Here's the president, the leader of
the Free World, and, just as that Latino store owner said, he's being
put through the same old wringer. So they're cheering for him, just as
blacks cheered for O.J.
This same wringer is bleakly displayed in the grand jury session.
The unwarranted release of the videotape, prompted by vehement
Republicans (maybe suckered by a White House pretending to dread
its broadcast), was an important event. For many years now defense
lawyers have fought for release of grand jury testimony, arguing that
only raw transcripts would show how prosecutors mischaracterize
testimony and draw up indictments on the basis of perversions of
statements made behind closed doors.
Clinton's and Monica Lewinsky's testimony entirely ratifies such
attacks on grand juries as presently used by prosecutors. Lewinsky,
for example, emerged from Starr's report to Congress as scheming
and manipulative. On Starr's account, one could almost build a case
against her as a shakedown artist. From the actual grand jury
transcript, however, a different and far more sympathetic picture of
Lewinsky emerges, one that prompted many of the jurors to muster
heartfelt expressions of sympathy and support.
Lewinsky told the grand jury several times she was never
encouraged to lie about her relationship with Clinton. Starr's report
omits these denials and says, deceptively, "Ms. Lewinsky has stated
that the president never explicitly told her to lie. Instead, as she
explained, they both understood from their conversations that they
would continue their pattern of covering up and lying about the
relationship."
Nor did Starr reflect in his report on Lewinsky's statement to the
grand jury that she'd told "a whole bunch of lies" to Linda Tripp,
including that she had told Vernon Jordan that she wouldn't sign an
affidavit saying she'd not had sex with Clinton until he, Jordan, got her
a job. This directly refutes a core claim of Starr, that the hunt for
Lewinsky's job was part of a larger pattern of obstruction of justice,
just like the famous "talking points," which was used to form a large
part of Starr's leaks and proclamations and which have now been
dropped.
A friend of mine who recently served on a grand jury said that the
accused always did better if they appeared before them. She found
that the only accused whose cases the jurors threw out were those
who came to testify. Their physical presence counterbalanced the
alleged victim or the cops.
So it turned out with Clinton. There he was, flesh and blood
(insofar as video can be flesh and blood), a human being facing the
often bizarre innuendoes of Starr's inquisition. Clinton's always been a
fake populist, so it's a wonderful irony that he may owe his survival in
office to genuine populism expressed in the revolt of public opinion
against the hypocrisy and cruelty of the justice system and the
hypocritical moralizing of the elites.
- - -
Alexander Cockburn Writes for the Nation and Other Publications

Thursday, September 24, 1998

Starr's Own Shading


Kenneth W. Starr's mandate as independent counsel was to
gather and evaluate evidence relating to possible wrongdoing
by President Clinton and to report to Congress any
information that might be a basis for impeachment. He was not to act
as judge and jury in assessing whether Clinton deserves a punishment
prescribed by the Constitution. That is solely Congress' responsibility.
Starr was to do his work free from partisan bias, as the "independent"
in his title is meant to signify. Now Clinton's lawyers charge that
Starr's report to Congress contains a "critical flaw" that deliberately
distorts the case against Clinton and raises doubts about its fairness
and the legal conclusions it draws. They have a point.
Two of the 11 potential grounds for impeachment cited in the
independent counsel's report stem from inferences that Clinton or
someone acting in his behalf asked Monica S. Lewinsky to lie about
their sexual relationship and that Lewinsky was promised a job in
exchange for her silence. If true, this would support allegations of
witness tampering and obstruction of justice. But in her testimony
before the grand jury Lewin-sky denied both allegations. The Starr
report's interpretation of her testimony is that Clinton "never
explicitly" told Lewinsky to lie or "explicitly" spelled out the job
proposal. In fact, Lewinsky swore in plain words that these things
never happened, and so far as is known there is no credible evidence
to contradict those assurances. The Starr report can do no better than
surmise that wrongdoing was accomplished indirectly, through winks
and nods. But where is the proof?
It is significant that in the grand jury room Starr's staff never
directly asked Lewinsky whether she had been urged to lie or had
been promised a job if she took part in a cover-up. It was left to a
grand juror to get Lewinsky's denial of these allegations on the
record, by asking whether she had anything more she wanted to say.
In an ordinary criminal case a prosecutor who hid potentially
exculpatory evidence from the defense would be in deep trouble. By
trying to minimize and obscure the significance of Lewinsky's denials,
who question his objectivity. None of this exonerates Clinton for his
behavior or excuses him from the lies he told. But it does seem to
weaken some of the case Starr has taken so long to construct and
should alert Congress that it would be wise to regard the Starr report
as something less than holy writ.


